authors.aff: Neo-Pythagorean philosopher of Tyana, Cappadocia
authors.sig: Neo-Pythagorean philosopher and traveling miracle worker from Tyana in Cappadocia. Most of what is told about him comes from Philostratus's partly legendary Life. A short treatise on prayer, angels, and true worship circulates under his name. Its authorship should be treated with caution.

authors.sig: Known only from one discourse, On Christ and the Churches. The Greek original is lost and the text survives in Georgian. Its exegesis resembles that of second-century Fathers, which argues against a later date.

authors.sig: Bishop of Lugdunum (Lyon) who wrote against the gnostics, especially Valentinus. He defended the four canonical gospels and the rule of faith handed down from the apostles. He taught that Christ recapitulates the ancient fashioning of Adam.

authors.sig: Teacher at Edessa who wrote hymns in Syriac and is called the father of Syriac poetry. His Book of the Laws of the Countries argues against astrological fatalism that free will is needed for morals, praise and blame. Later writers judged him heretical because his star speculation was mixed with his Christianity.

authors.sig: Presbyter of the church at Rome, exiled with Bishop Pontianus to Sardinia in 235. He wrote commentaries on the blessings of Isaac and Jacob and of Moses, reading them as prophecies of Christ's descent and obedience on the cross.

w: On Free Will: Greek Text (De autexusio : texte grec) · PO 22
On Free Will: Slavonic Version (De autexusio : version slave) · PO 22
authors.aff: Bishop of Olympus (Lycia)
authors.sig: On Free Will defends human freedom of choice against determinism and Manichaean dualism, arguing that God is not the author of evil and that matter is not eternal or uncreated — a key patristic witness on evil, creation, and providence.

w: Demonstration XXIII on the Grape (Demonstratio XXIII de Acino) · PS 2
authors.aff: Mar Mattai Monastery near Mosul; possibly a bishop
authors.sig: Persian Sage of the Syriac church who wrote twenty-three Demonstrations between about 336 and 345 for his monastic colleagues. They are the earliest surviving body of Syriac Christian theology, expounding sin, prayer, Christology, the church, virtues, and last things. Many turn against Jewish positions, drawing on Isaiah, Paul, Jeremiah, and Moses.

authors.aff: Bishop (Patriarch) of Alexandria, 8 June 328 – 2 May 373
authors.sig: The chief fourth-century opponent of Arianism, called the 'Father of Orthodoxy'. His writings argue that the Son is begotten, not made, and consubstantial with the Father, shaping Trinitarian doctrine.

authors.aff: Deacon of Nisibis, later of Edessa
authors.sig: Deacon of Nisibis and later of Edessa, he wrote hymns and verse homilies on sin, providence, and prayer. His memre on Nicomedia survive in Syriac and Armenian. Many works later circulated under his name, so authorship must be weighed case by case.

authors.aff: Bishop of Constantia (Salamis), Cyprus
authors.sig: Bishop of Constantia (Salamis) on Cyprus from 367 for nearly forty years. He wrote the Panarion, a compendium of eighty heresies. Its chapter on heresy LXXX attacks the Messalians. He treats them as a new sect named for their excessive praying.

authors.aff: Anchorite and bishop; successor of Anthony at Pispir
authors.sig: His letters are among the few documents that attest the mysticism of the desert fathers. They center on the acquisition of the Spirit, purification, and illumination. They are independent of Evagrius Ponticus and basically biblical in origin.

w: Syriac Extracts of the Historia Monachorum (Deux extraits de la version syriaque de l'Historia monachorum de Rufin) · PO 11
authors.aff: Monastery on the Mount of Olives, Jerusalem
authors.sig: His translation of the Historia monachorum carried the lives and sayings of the Egyptian ascetics to the Latin West; the excerpts here treat conquering sinful inclinations gradually ('little by little') and raising the dead by prayer.

authors.aff: Monk of Nitria and Kellia, Egyptian desert
authors.sig: A desert monk who supported himself by copying manuscripts at Nitria and Kellia in Egypt. His Kephalaia Gnostica sets out his speculative theology in short definitional chapters. Most of his Greek originals are lost. His writings survive chiefly in Syriac, Armenian, and Latin translations.

w: Four Homilies on the Temptations and Incarnation · PO 13
authors.aff: Archbishop of Constantinople
authors.sig: Archbishop of Constantinople, known for his sermons against the misuse of wealth, and later exiled. His four homilies on the temptations of Christ and the Incarnation argue that Christ's fast and temptation reverse Adam's fall. Adam and Christ were tempted alike through food, and Christ overcomes the devil in the body he assumed.

w: Controversy with the Macedonians (Théodore de Mopsueste : Controverse avec les Macédoniens) · PO 9
authors.aff: Bishop of Mopsuestia in Cilicia, 392–428
authors.sig: Bishop of Mopsuestia in Cilicia from 392 to 428, and an exegete of the Antiochene school. He wrote a polemic against the Macedonians defending the full divinity and co-equality of the Holy Spirit against those who ranked him with creatures. The Fifth General Council condemned him posthumously in 553.

authors.aff: Abbot of a monastery near Ancyra
authors.sig: Abbot of a monastery near Ancyra, he wrote treatises on moral and ascetic subjects and more than a thousand letters. His Epistle on Voluntary Poverty to Magna teaches that idleness stirs up the passions and that prayer without inner reality perishes.

w: Letter to Amphilochius of Side · PS 3
authors.aff: Patriarch of Alexandria (412–444)
authors.sig: Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444 and a central opponent of Nestorius. In Against Nestorius and the Explanation of the Twelve Chapters he argued that one Christ is God and man and that the Word suffered in the flesh. His treatise That the Virgin is Theotokos argues that Mary is truly Theotokos.

authors.aff: Bishop of Bagrevand (probable); pupil of Isaac the Great and Mesrop Mashtots
authors.sig: Probably bishop of Bagrevand, he was a pupil of Mesrop Mashtots and helped translate the Armenian Bible. His only surviving work, On God, refutes pagans, Magi, Greek philosophers, Marcionites, and Manichaeans. It defends creation out of nothing and free will against Iranian dualism.

authors.aff: Bishop of Ancyra

authors.aff: Bishop of Cyrrhus (from c. 423)
authors.sig: Bishop of Cyrrhus from about 423 and a defender of the Antiochene side against Cyril of Alexandria. His Philotheus historia recounts the lives of Syrian ascetics and presents their intercession and discipline as models of true worship.

w: Hesychius of Jerusalem: Homilies I-XI · PO 42
Hesychius of Jerusalem: Homilies XII-XXIV · PO 42
authors.aff: Priest and didascale (catechist) of the Church of Jerusalem
authors.sig: Presbyter and teacher of the Church of Jerusalem in the first half of the fifth century. Chroniclers recognized him as the chief biblical interpreter of Jerusalem and Palestine. His Homilies on Job defend Job against his friends and the devil, and treat sin, providence, and endurance under trial. Only an Armenian version of them survives.

w: Narsaï's metrical homilies on the nativity, epiphany, passion, resurrection and ascension · PO 40
authors.aff: School of Nisibis (director, 471–496); formerly School of Edessa
authors.sig: Director of the School of Nisibis from 471 to about 496, after he taught exegesis at Edessa. Eighty-one of his metrical homilies survive. He argues that God created from nothing by his word in an instant. Angels mediate providence in his verse exegesis.

w: Arabic Life of Dioscorus (Die arabische Version der Vita Dioscori) · PO 56
authors.aff: Disciple of Dioscorus I of Alexandria
authors.sig: His Life of Dioscorus is the principal anti-Chalcedonian narrative of Dioscorus's trial and exile, defending him against Leo of Rome, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Nestorius, and the council's 'unbelieving bishop.'

authors.aff: Bishop of Maypherqat (Martyropolis), Mesopotamia
authors.sig: Bishop of Maypherqat in Mesopotamia, he gathered martyrs' relics into his city. He pleaded the cause of the persecuted Persian church at Constantinople and served as envoy to the shah for Theodosius II. His heresiological catalogue treats the Trinity and the Church and marks him as an early Syriac polemicist.

authors.aff: Bishop of Antioch in Pisidia
authors.sig: Bishop of Antioch in Pisidia around 440 and a Miaphysite. He wrote a Nativity discourse known only in Syriac and an Epiphany sermon preached at Constantinople before Patriarch Proclus, which survives as excerpts in florilegia.

w: Extracts of Timothy Aelurus (Extraits de Timothée Ælure) · PO 13
authors.aff: Patriarch of Alexandria (non-Chalcedonian), 457–460 and 475–477
authors.sig: Patriarch of Alexandria in 457–460 and again from 475 until his death in 477, he opposed the Council of Chalcedon. His Homily on the Church of the Rock attacks Chalcedon, Nestorius, and Leo of Rome, and survives in Coptic, Arabic, and Ethiopian versions.

authors.aff: Metropolitan bishop of Mabbug (Hierapolis), 485–519
authors.sig: Metropolitan bishop of Mabbug from 485 to 519, he championed Miaphysitism against the Nestorians and dyophysites. He sponsored a Philoxenian New Testament translated from the Greek. His Letter to Patricius argues that Christ took his body from the virgin and that God himself suffered on the cross.

authors.aff: Bishop of Batnan da-Srug (519–521)
authors.sig: Bishop of Batnan da-Srug from 519 until his death in 521. He wrote several hundred verse homilies in a twelve-syllable meter, of which about 400 survive. His homilies argue from prophecy and typology that Christ is the true Son promised to Israel, and they oppose Jewish claims and the obligation to keep the Sabbath.

authors.aff: Bishop of Mytilene
authors.sig: Bishop of Mytilene on Lesbos. His Ecclesiastical History survives in Syriac under the name Pseudo-Zacharias Rhetor. The excerpt relating to Severus of Antioch cites Severus more heavily than any other authority. It argues that patristic doctrine settles Christ's bodily incorruptibility.

authors.aff: Patriarch of Antioch, 512–518
authors.sig: Patriarch of Antioch from 512 until his deposition in 518. He died in exile in Egypt in 538. His homilies and letters survive largely in Syriac. They defend the one incarnate nature of God the Word against Nestorius and Eutyches.

authors.aff: Bishop (metropolitan) of Mytilene; formerly lawyer at Constantinople
authors.sig: Bishop of Mytilene on Lesbos and formerly a lawyer at Constantinople. He wrote the Life of Severus. It defends Severus of Antioch's episcopal conduct and innocence against slanderers, pagans and Manichaeans.

w: IV. Plerophories: Testimonies and Revelations against the Council of Chalcedon · PO 8
authors.aff: Bishop of Maiuma at Gaza
authors.sig: Anti-Chalcedonian presbyter and monk who later served the altar at a monastery in Maiuma. He wrote the Plerophories, which gathers testimonies and revelations against the Council of Chalcedon and calls its two-natures Christology heresy.

authors.aff: Court of Constantinople; chancellor to Justinian
authors.sig: The extracts here come from his Chronicle, a chief Latin continuation of Eusebius covering the Eastern Empire from Theodosius I to Justinian's reign.

w: Acts of the Synod of 486 (XXVII-XXVIII. Ex actis synodi anno 486 praeside Mâr Acacio habitae) · PS 3
authors.aff: Synod of 486 under Catholicos Acacius of Seleucia-Ctesiphon
authors.sig: The 486 acts are among the earliest documentary records of the Church of the East's self-definition, showing it legislating discipline and doctrine against wandering monks and local heretics a generation after the Council of Chalcedon.

authors.aff: Probably a jurist at Antioch; later moved to Constantinople
authors.sig: Byzantine chronicler of Syrian origin, born at Antioch around 491. He was probably a jurist there before moving to Constantinople under Justinian I. His 18-book Chronographia is a world history from Creation to Justinian's reign. It created the type of the Byzantine chronicle.

authors.aff: Hermitage near the monastery of Abba Seridus, Gaza, Palestine
authors.sig: Their correspondence is a principal witness to sixth-century Gaza monastic spiritual direction and shaped later Orthodox monasticism through Elder Paisius Velichkovsky's Slavonic translation and the Optina elders' modern Russian versions.

authors.aff: Archdeacon of Carthage
authors.sig: Archdeacon of Carthage who went to Rome in 535 as legate of an African synod of 217 bishops to consult Pope Agapetus I. He wrote the Breviarium causae Nestorianorum et Eutychianorum, a Chalcedonian history of the Nestorian and Monophysite controversies that argues Justinian's condemnation was misjudged.

authors.aff: Lector (reader) at Hagia Sophia, Constantinople
authors.sig: His continuation is one of the few surviving sources for the church history of the late fifth and early sixth centuries, and these excerpts preserve his anti-Miaphysite account of the reign of Anastasius.

authors.aff: Titular Bishop of Ephesus; active in Constantinople
authors.sig: Titular Bishop of Ephesus, he worked mainly among the miaphysite community in Constantinople and was imprisoned under Justin II. He wrote Lives of the Eastern Saints, some 58 lives that admit only miracles attested by eyewitnesses. In them he argues against Chalcedon and maintains that tested virtue qualifies a man for spiritual office.

authors.aff: Titular bishop of Ephesus and miaphysite leader in Constantinople
authors.sig: A miaphysite leader in Constantinople who was imprisoned repeatedly after 571 and wrote the Lives of the Eastern Saints and part of an Ecclesiastical History. A Life of James is attributed to him, but whether he wrote it is uncertain. It defends miaphysite hierarchy against Chalcedonian bishops.

w: Homily for the Feast of the Annunciation · PO 16
Homily for the Feast of the Hypapante · PO 16
authors.aff: Archbishop of Ephesus
authors.sig: His two surviving homilies — on the Annunciation and on the Hypapante — are important evidence for the history of the Byzantine liturgy and the gradual reception of the feasts; the Annunciation homily defends preaching on March 25 against earlier custom (in which no father had preached on the Annunciation) and argues that Christ himself accomplished salvation.

authors.aff: Monasteries of the Judaean desert, Palestine, including the monastery of Euthymius the Great, the New Lavra
authors.sig: His Life of Saint Sabas is both a primary source for Palestinian desert monasticism and a Chalcedonian polemic: it insists communion requires accepting Chalcedon and condemning Eutyches, and it argues against Emperor Anastasius, Severus of Antioch, and the Acephali.

authors.aff: advocate at Antioch, aide to Patriarch Gregory of Antioch
authors.sig: His is the last continuation of the Eusebian church-history series and a principal source for the Nestorian, Eutychian, and late Monophysite controversies; the excerpts here document the account of Severus of Antioch's fall.

Treatise on the Martyrs (Traité sur les martyrs) · PO 7
authors.aff: Interpreter of the school of Seleucia-Ctesiphon
authors.sig: Interpreter at the school of Seleucia-Ctesiphon and a disciple of Aba I, he flourished in the mid-sixth century. His Treatise on the Martyrs answers those who call the veneration of martyrs idolatry, arguing that honor paid to martyrs' bones is not latria and that commemoration profits the living.

w: Treatise on Golden Friday (Traité sur le Vendredi d'Or) · PO 7
Treatise on the Rogations (Traité sur les Rogations) · PO 7
authors.aff: Director of the School of Nisibis (571/572–610)
authors.sig: Director of the School of Nisibis from about 571 or 572 until his death around 610. He broke with the Antiochene exegesis of Theodore of Mopsuestia and followed John Chrysostom, which divided the Church of the East. Only his treatises on the Golden Friday and the Rogations survive complete.

w: Chronicle of Victor of Tunnuna · PO 2
authors.aff: Bishop of Tunnuna (North Africa)
authors.sig: Bishop of Tunnuna in North Africa and chronicler. He backed the Three Chapters and refused Justinian's edict of 544. He was imprisoned, exiled and confined in a Constantinople monastery. His Chronicle defends Chalcedon. Only the part from 444 survives.

w: Letter to Arcadius of Cyprus (Lettre à Arcadius de Chypre) · PO 39
Panegyric of Saints Cyrus and John (Panégyrique des Saints Cyr et Jean) · PO 51
authors.aff: Patriarch of Jerusalem (634–638)
authors.sig: Patriarch of Jerusalem from 634 and the chief opponent of monothelism. He wrote a Chalcedonian polemic against the Nestorians and the Eutychians. He held that only the Son suffered on the cross.

w: Acts of the Synod of 576 · PS 3
Scholia on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy · PS 3
authors.aff: Monk and abbot of Chrysopolis; former first secretary to Emperor Heraclius
authors.sig: Monk and abbot of Chrysopolis who opposed Monothelitism, the imperial teaching of a single will in Christ. He wrote the Questions to Thalassius and the Mystagogy, and his commentaries on Pseudo-Dionysius shaped later medieval theology and mysticism.

w: On Those Who Approach the Church · PS 3
authors.aff: Presbyter of Hagia Sophia, Constantinople
authors.sig: Presbyter of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, active around 600 or 700. He wrote On Those Who Enter the Church, a Greek handbook on receiving heretics that sorts them by the rite each group needs. Theodore the Studite later used the same three categories.

w: Acts of the Synod of 585 (XXX-XXXI. Ex actis synodi anno 585 praeside Iesuiahb I habitae) · PS 3
Cause of the Foundation of Schools (Cause de la fondation des écoles) · PO 4

Ecclesiastical History I (I, chapitres I à XVIII) · PO 23
authors.aff: School of Nisibis, during the directorship of Ḥenana of Adiabene
authors.sig: His two surviving works are among the most important sources for the School of Nisibis. They give an East Syrian account of the Arian controversy and the Cyril–Nestorius dispute.

w: Chronicle of Jacob of Edessa · PO 2
authors.aff: Bishop of Edessa (ca. 684–689, briefly restored 708)
authors.sig: Bishop of Edessa from about 684 and a Syriac Orthodox writer of the late seventh century. His Chronicle survives in part and gives a Miaphysite account of Severus of Antioch, who succeeded Flavian as bishop of Antioch and was driven out after Justin accepted Chalcedon.

w: Homily on Psalm 6 (Omelia sul Salmo 6) · PO 52
authors.aff: Abbot of St Catherine's Monastery, Mount Sinai
authors.sig: Abbot of Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai, he wrote a Homily on Psalm 6 that treats the psalm as the foundation of repentance. He argues that true repentance requires humble, tearful confession and that mercy to the unworthy glorifies God most.

w: Life of Isaac, Patriarch of Alexandria (Vie d'Isaac, Patriarche d'Alexandrie de 686 à 689) · PO 11
authors.aff: Bishop of Pchati
authors.sig: His life of Isaac is the principal Coptic narrative source for the patriarchate of 686–689. It is hagiography written by a near-contemporary bishop.

w: John of Damascus: Compendium of Heresies · PS 3
authors.aff: Monk and priest, Mar Saba monastery near Jerusalem
authors.sig: Monk and priest at Mar Saba near Jerusalem, he defended the veneration of icons against the iconoclast emperor Leo III. His Exposition of the Orthodox Faith systematized Greek dogmatic theology, and he wrote the Three Treatises on the Divine Images.

w: The Letters of John of Dalyatha (La collection des lettres de Jean de Dalyatha) · PO 39
authors.aff: Monk and abbot, Qardu mountains
authors.sig: Monk who adopted the eremitic life in the mountains of Beth Dalyatha. In old age a group of monks made him their abbot at Qardu. His letters trace the mystical path from repentance through purity to perfection. They teach that God reveals himself inwardly to those who love him.

w: Letter on the Three Stages of Monastic Life (Lettre sur les trois étapes de la vie monastique) · PO 45
authors.aff: Abbot of the monastery of Rabban Bakhtishoʿ, Adiabene
authors.sig: Abbot of Rabban Bakhtishoʿ in Adiabene. He taught a three-stage itinerary of monastic life, the somatic, the psychic and the spiritual. His Centuries and his letter on those stages set out East Syriac teaching on prayer, grace and sanctification against demons.

authors.aff: Monk, monastery near Cyzicus
authors.sig: His annals are the leading source for seventh- and eighth-century Byzantine history, and the excerpts here preserve a Chalcedonian polemical account of the Severus-Anastasius-Anthimus crises.

w: Scholia of Theodore bar Konai (XIX-XX. Ex libro XI scholiorum Theodori bar Chôni) · PS 3
authors.aff: Teacher (malfānā) from Kaškar, Mesopotamia
authors.sig: Teacher from Kaškar who wrote the Book of Scholia in 791–792. The work comments on the whole Bible and includes an apology for Christian teaching. Book XI treats the Messalian movement, which arose among Edessene monks.

authors.aff: Chief physician to Caliph al-Mutawakkil, Baghdad
authors.sig: Chief physician to Caliph al-Mutawakkil in Baghdad. He translated Greek medical and philosophical works into Syriac and Arabic. His side of an Arabic correspondence with Ibn al-Munajjim argues over Scripture, true worship and God's knowledge.

w: On the Synod of Side · PS 3
authors.aff: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople (858–867, 877–886)
authors.sig: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople in two periods, 858 to 867 and 877 to 886. He wrote an account of the Synod of Side, convened against the Messalian heresy. It argues that convicted heretics may be deposed from office and that defenders of a heretic share his condemnation.

w: Homily on the Girdle of the Virgin · PO 16
Homily on the Conception of Anne · PO 16
First Homily on the Conception of Saint Anne · PO 19
authors.aff: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople (February 907 – 15 May 912)
authors.sig: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 907 to 912 and spiritual father to Emperor Leo VI. He refused to enter Leo's fourth wife in the diptychs and was deposed in May 912. His homilies on the Virgin's girdle at Chalcopratia and on the conception of Anne assert the veneration of relics and Mary as Mother of God.

w: Homily on the Dormition of the Virgin · PO 16
authors.aff: Archimandrite of a monastery in Constantinople
authors.sig: Byzantine monk and archimandrite of a Constantinople monastery who went to Rome to defend his patriarch. He wrote a homily on the Dormition of the Virgin in which an angel announces her death and she accepts it willingly, and it carries anti-Jewish polemic.

w: Funeral Oration for Saint Euthymius (Oraison funèbre de saint Euthyme par Aréthas de Césarée) · PO 16
authors.aff: Archbishop of Caesarea Mazaca (Cappadocia), early 10th century
authors.sig: Archbishop of Caesarea Mazaca in Cappadocia and a scholar of the Macedonian Renaissance. He compiled the oldest extant Greek scholia on the Apocalypse. His Funeral Oration of Saint Euthymius defends the saint's unjust deposition and exile. It argues from Scripture and ascetic discipline to the blessedness of the righteous.

w: Athanasius of Alexandria, Third Oration against the Arians (Athanasius of Alexandria, Oratio III contra Arianos) · PO 58
authors.aff: Preslav Literary School, First Bulgarian Empire
authors.sig: Scholar and translator at the Preslav Literary School who wrote the Didactic Gospel, the first systematic sermon book in Slavic. In 906 Tsar Simeon I commissioned his Old Bulgarian translation of Athanasius of Alexandria's anti-Arian works.

w: Universal History Part I, I · PO 5
Universal History Part I, II · PO 11
authors.aff: Bishop of Manbij (Hierapolis) in Syria
authors.sig: Bishop of Manbij in Syria. He wrote the Kitāb al-ʿUnwān in Arabic, a universal history from the foundation of the world. He drew on Syriac sources and on Eusebius. He was the first Eastern writer to call Tatian a heretic.

authors.sig: Bishop of Hermopolis Magna in Upper Egypt around the end of the tenth century. He wrote theology in Arabic because Egyptian Christians no longer knew Coptic, and his homilies defend Miaphysite Christology against Nestorius and Arius. He also refuted Saʿîd Ibn-Batriq's Book of Councils.

authors.aff: Physician in Byzantine-held Antioch, exiled from Fatimid Egypt
authors.sig: Physician and historian who fled Fatimid Egypt for Byzantine-held Antioch. His continuation of Eutychius' Annals covers 938 to 1034 and is a principal source for al-Hakim's persecutions and eleventh-century Byzantine-Arab affairs. events: Bardaisan at Edessa
A Christian teacher at the court of Edessa argues in Syriac for free will against fate and the stars.
The Council of Nicaea
The first general council meets in Bithynia.
Aphrahat’s Demonstrations
In the Persian empire the “Persian Sage” writes twenty-three discourses, dated between 337 and 345.
Nisibis given up to Persia
Ephrem leaves Nisibis for Edessa, where he dies ten years later.
Letters for Armenian
Mesrop Mashtots makes an alphabet for Armenian; Eznik of Kolb is among his pupils.
The Council of Ephesus
Nestorius is condemned, and Mary is confessed Theotokos, the Mother of God.
The Council of Chalcedon
Christ is confessed in two natures. Many in Egypt and Syria refuse the definition, and in time the churches divide.
From Edessa to Nisibis
The emperor Zeno closes the school of the Persians at Edessa; its teachers go to Narsai’s school at Nisibis, across the Persian border.
Severus at Antioch
A monk of Maiuma becomes patriarch of Antioch. Deposed in 518, he dies in Egypt in 538.
A hierarchy of their own
Jacob Baradaeus begins to ordain bishops and priests for the opponents of Chalcedon in Syria.
The Arab conquests
Jerusalem, Syria and Mesopotamia pass to the Arabs, and Egypt by 642. In time the churches of the East write in Arabic as well.
Baghdad
The catholicos of the Church of the East settles in the caliphs’ new city, where Hunayn ibn Ishaq will later serve the caliph as physician.
al-Biruni
A Muslim scholar of Khwarazm describes the feasts each Christian sect keeps in the Syrian months.
The Armenian synaxary
Ter Israel compiles the Armenian book of the saints for each day of the year.
Bar Hebraeus
The great scholar of the Syriac Orthodox Church is made its maphrian of the East.
The Council of Florence
The Greek bishops accept union with Rome; Mark of Ephesus refuses to sign.
Constantinople falls
Gennadius Scholarios, Mark’s pupil, becomes the first patriarch under the Ottomans.
Paul of Aleppo
The archdeacon of Antioch travels north with his father, the patriarch Macarius, and writes the journey in Arabic.

biruni.src: القول على ما يستعمله النصارى الملكائية فى الشهور السزيانية والنصارى مفترقون فرقا فالاولى منهم الملكائية وهم الروم وانما سموا بذلك لان ملك الروم على …
biruni.en: Christians are divided into several sects. The first is that of the Melkites: these are the Greeks, and they are so called for the sole reason that the emperor (malik) of the Greeks follows their cult. It alone extends over the empire. The second is that of the Nestorians, whose name is linked to Nestorius, the founder of their system, in the year 720 and some of Alexander. The third is that of the Jacobites.

keys_say: Where to begin on this shelf. The groups are the writers of each church, the Greek writers whose works the series prints in Eastern versions and two Muslim scholars. Each group runs in the order they wrote.

keys.label: Edessa and Persia
keys.say: The first writers in Syriac, before the councils divided the churches. They are a teacher at the court of Edessa, a sage of the Persian church and the deacon of Nisibis and Edessa.

keys.label: Against Chalcedon
keys.say: Bishops and monks of Egypt and Syria who refused the council of 451, and the Syriac Orthodox scholars after them.

keys.label: The Church of the East
keys.say: The church of the Persian empire. Here are its school at Nisibis, its monks in the mountains of Adiabene and Qardu and its scholars under the caliphs.

keys.label: Egypt
keys.say: A hermit of the desert and a Coptic bishop’s life of a patriarch. Then come the Copts who wrote in Arabic under the caliphs and the sultans.

keys.label: Armenia
keys.say: An Armenian bishop of the first generation that wrote the language, and the compiler of its book of the saints.

keys.label: Greek writers in Eastern versions
keys.say: Greek Fathers whose works survive in Eastern versions. The series prints them in Armenian, Georgian, Syriac or Slavonic.

keys.label: Chalcedonians
keys.say: Writers of the churches that kept the council. They include Jerusalem and Sinai, the Arabic historians of Antioch and the Greeks at Florence.

keys.label: Outside the churches
keys.say: Two Muslim scholars who described the Christians’ feasts, and a pagan philosopher to whom a short work on talismans is ascribed.

keyworks.say: The books the series is known for in the order they were written. They run from Irenaeus in Armenian to Mark of Ephesus at Florence.

works.note: A short account of the faith written for his friend Marcianus. The whole text is known only in Armenian.
